issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on common intention is not invalid merely because no specific charge alleging common intention was framed when the accused received notice of the case and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 of the Penal Code, but were also convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 without a specific charge under Section 34.

The circumstances showing concert and participation in the joint criminal action were put to the appellants in their examination under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Court found that they understood the case against them.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a specific charge under Section 34 did not invalidate the trial because the appellants were aware of the case they had to meet and no prejudice arose.
issues.legal_principle: Under Willie (William) Slaney v. State of Madhya Pradesh, explaining Nanak Chand v. State of Punjab, the purpose of a charge is to give the accused notice of the matter alleged; a defect in the charge does not invalidate the trial absent prejudice causing a failure of justice. The Court also referred to Section 535 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

predicates.criminal_trial_without_specific_common_i: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused is convicted on a common-intention basis without a specific charge alleging common intention.
predicates.common_action_circumstances_put_to_accus: The circumstances said to show concert and participation in the joint criminal action were put to the accused during the trial.
predicates.accused_understood_case: The accused understood the matter they were being tried for.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial proceeds without a specific common-intention charge, the conviction is not invalidated by that omission if the joint-action circumstances were put to the accused and the accused understood the case.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal in a separate proceeding does not create issue estoppel on a fact that the earlier court did not decide.
material_facts: The accused was tried for murder in one proceeding and separately for an offence concerning possession of the same gun under the Arms Act.
The murder proceeding was decided before the Arms Act proceeding.
The accused admitted in both proceedings that the gun had been recovered from his possession.

The acquittal in the Arms Act proceeding rested on failure to prove an intention to use the gun, or allow its use, for an unlawful purpose; the trial judge made no finding that the accused had not possessed the gun.
issues.conclusion: The Arms Act acquittal did not prevent the murder court from finding that the accused possessed the gun.
issues.legal_principle: The issue-estoppel doctrine discussed in Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab did not apply because the earlier acquittal did not determine the disputed fact of possession. The Court also considered A.P. State v. Meerayya and Manipur Administration v. Thokchom Birasingh, which had been cited by the defence.

predicates.murder_trial_and_separate_related_trial: The accused faced a murder proceeding and a separate related proceeding concerning the same item or conduct.
predicates.accused_admitted_possession: The accused admitted in the proceedings that the item had been recovered from their possession.
predicates.earlier_acquittal_did_not_decide_possess: The earlier acquittal rested on a different unproved element and did not determine whether the accused possessed the item.

issues.definition: When a person admitted possession and an acquittal in a separate related proceeding did not decide possession, that acquittal does not bar a finding of possession in the murder trial.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not normally disturb concurrent factual findings in a special-leave appeal unless grave and exceptional circumstances disclose a failure of justice.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The lower courts had concurrently convicted the appellants for the murders of three victims.
The Supreme Court found no circumstances of sufficient gravity to warrant interference with those convictions.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for those three murders were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its special jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court does not normally reappraise evidence or disturb concurrent findings of fact unless grave and exceptional circumstances exist and there has been a failure of justice.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not grave_exceptional_failure_of_justice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower courts reached the same factual findings on the convictions under review.
predicates.grave_exceptional_failure_of_justice: The concurrent findings are affected by grave and exceptional circumstances resulting in a failure of justice.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, concurrent factual findings are left undisturbed when grave and exceptional circumstances resulting in a failure of justice are absent.

issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction cannot be sustained on a merely plausible prosecution explanation when the medical and other evidence fails to provide positive and convincing proof of the accused's responsibility.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that a gunshot aimed at one victim passed through his neck and killed another victim.
The medical evidence described triangular wounds, and the doctor could not rule out that they were caused by a sharp-pointed weapon.
The expected signs and surrounding evidence of a close-range gunshot were absent, and the victim who was allegedly targeted had no gunshot injury.

The accused had said at the earliest stage that the victim was killed by a sharp-pointed weapon used by the complainant party; the doctor’s opinion and the other circumstances supported that possibility.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the appellants’ convictions for the murder of that victim because the prosecution had not established its account with positive and convincing proof.
issues.legal_principle: A conviction must rest on positive and convincing proof; a plausible explanation alone is insufficient where the medical and surrounding evidence supports a materially different account of how the fatal injury was caused.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a murder conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_not_convincing: The prosecution evidence does not provide positive and convincing proof of the accused's responsibility for the death.
predicates.evidence_supports_alternative_cause: Medical or other evidence supports a materially different explanation for the fatal injury.

issues.definition: On appeal from a murder conviction, the conviction is set aside when the prosecution proof is not convincing and the evidence supports an alternative cause of death.

issues.legal_issue: Possible sudden armed combat and prolonged exposure to an impending execution may be considered in choosing life imprisonment rather than death, even when they do not establish private defence or otherwise excuse the offence.
material_facts: The accused had serious injuries, including an injury from a sharp-pointed weapon to a vital part of the body, which the prosecution did not explain.
The deceased and their companions carried weapons, and the evidence left open the possibility that gunfire began after the accused had been assaulted in a sudden encounter.
The circumstances did not establish private defence or otherwise excuse the offences, but the death sentences had remained pending for an extended period.
issues.conclusion: The Court commuted the death sentences to imprisonment for life, taking account of the possible sudden armed encounter and the prolonged period under the threat of execution.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding between death and life imprisonment, circumstances that do not establish private defence or excuse the offence may still be considered as mitigating factors. The Court relied on the possible sudden combat and the prolonged dread of impending execution; it cited no statute or earlier case for this sentencing determination.

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and unexplained_serious_injuries_to_accused and possible_sudden_armed_combat and prolonged_impending_execution

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a death sentence.
predicates.unexplained_serious_injuries_to_accused: The accused had serious injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
predicates.possible_sudden_armed_combat: The circumstances leave open the possibility of a sudden encounter involving armed groups and an exchange of violence.
predicates.prolonged_impending_execution: The condemned person endured a prolonged period under the threat of execution.

issues.definition: A death sentence is commuted to life imprisonment when an appeal involves unexplained serious injuries to the accused, possible sudden armed combat, and a prolonged period under the threat of execution.
